sections.h: Psalms 102–106: the end of Book IV
sections.b: Book IV (Psalms 90–106) opens with "A prayer of Moses" (Psalm 90) and closes with two psalms that retell the age of Moses: Psalm 105 as God's faithfulness, Psalm 106 as Israel's sin. Between them, Psalm 102 sets human frailty against God's endless years, and Psalms 103 and 104 form a pair framed by "Bless the LORD, my soul," moving from God's mercy to Israel to his care for every creature. The book ends with the doxology of Psalm 106:48, which 1 Chronicles 16:36 quotes, and "Praise the LORD!" (Hallelujah) appears for the first time in the Psalter at Psalm 104:35. Gerald Wilson argued that Book IV answers the crisis of the Davidic kingship mourned in Psalm 89 by turning back to Moses and to God's own kingship.

common: Each of the first four books of the Psalter ends with a short blessing of God; Book IV's is Psalm 106:48.
uncommon: Chronicles quotes the end of Book IV, which suggests that the Psalter's division into books was known by about 400–300 BC.

sections.h: Psalm 104:35: let sinners be finished off
sections.b: Psalm 104, a hymn of joy in creation, ends with a short curse: "Let sinners be finished off from the earth, / and let the wicked be gone for good" (Psalm 104:35). The Talmud tells how Rabbi Meir wanted to pray for the death of some ruffians, and his wife Beruriah answered that the verse can be read "let sins be finished off" (chata'im for chatta'im), so that he should pray for them to repent, and then "the wicked" would be no more (Bavli Berakhot 10a). Psalm 106 has no curse, but it tells how God himself handed the people over to their enemies (Psalm 106:41–42).

common: Psalm 104 ends with a wish that sinners vanish from the earth.
uncommon: Beruriah's reading turns the curse into a prayer for repentance.

sections.b: Psalm 104 is the Bible's longest poem about creation. It touches each of the six days of Genesis 1, roughly in order (though its animals and birds come before the sun and moon), and tells them in the present tense: God wraps himself in light, waters the mountains, makes grass grow, feeds lions and people, and gives breath. When he takes back the breath of his creatures they die, and when he sends it out "they are created" (Psalm 104:29–30), so that creation is renewed every day. Psalm 102:25–26 adds that the earth and heavens God made will wear out like clothing while he remains, a text Hebrews 1:10–12 applies to the Son.

common: Psalm 104 loosely follows the order of the days of Genesis 1.
uncommon: Many scholars think part of Psalm 104 is modeled on an Egyptian hymn to the sun god Aten.

sections.h: Psalm 104 and the order of the days
sections.b: Psalm 104 follows the sequence of Genesis 1 loosely, though not exactly, since its wild animals and birds (104:11–12, 17–18) come before the sun and moon: light (104:2), sky and upper waters (104:2–4), the waters driven back and dry land (104:5–9), plants (104:14–17), sun and moon for the appointed times (104:19), the sea and its creatures (104:25–26), animals and people fed (104:21–23, 27–28). It is often cited by readers who take the days as a literary framework, because the psalm keeps the order but not a week, and by those who take them as literal, because it confirms the order. It does not settle the question either way.

sections.h: Psalm 104 and the Great Hymn to the Aten
sections.b: The Great Hymn to the Aten, carved in the tomb of Ay at Amarna in the reign of Akhenaten (about 1350–1334 BC), praises the sun disk as the one creator. Scholars since Breasted have noted parallels with Psalm 104:20–30: night and lions, morning and human work, ships and sea creatures, all life depending on the god's rising and setting, and an exclamation at how many are his works. Some, like John Day, think the psalmist knew a form of the hymn; others, like James Hoffmeier, think both reflect shared ways of praising a creator. Psalm 104 also uses Canaanite storm-god imagery: God rides the clouds and rebukes the waters (104:3, 7), as Baal does in the texts from Ugarit.

common: Psalm 104 has close parallels with an Egyptian hymn to the sun.
uncommon: The psalm makes the sun a creature that "knows where it sets" rather than a god.

sections.b: Hebrews 1:10–12 quotes Psalm 102:25–27 from the Greek as words spoken to the Son: he laid the earth's foundation, the heavens are his handiwork, and he remains the same when they wear out. The Greek adds the address "Lord," which the Hebrew lacks. Most churches read the passage as a witness that the Son is the Creator and true God; Jehovah's Witnesses read it of the Son as God's agent in creation; Latter-day Saints identify Christ with the Jehovah of the Old Testament.

sections.h: The heavens wear out like clothing
sections.b: Psalm 102:25–27 says that the earth and heavens will "be lost" and be changed like clothing, while God remains. Isaiah 51:6 uses the same picture, and Isaiah 65:17 and Isaiah 66:22 speak of new heavens and a new earth. Christian readers have linked the psalm to 2 Peter 3:10–13 and Revelation 21:1. Some take it to mean the world will be destroyed and replaced, others that it will be renewed, as a garment is changed. Psalm 104:30, "you make the surface of the ground new," uses the same verb of renewal for every spring.

sections.b: Psalm 103:3 puts forgiveness and healing side by side: "He pardons every wrong you have done; / he heals every sickness you have." The word for sickness, tachalu'im, is used of physical illness (Deuteronomy 29:22; 2 Chronicles 21:19). The psalm's list moves on to rescue from the Pit and renewed youth (103:4–5), so most readers take it as thanks after recovery from a serious illness. Pentecostal churches cite it, with Isaiah 53:4–5 and James 5:14–15, for divine healing as part of the gospel; Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed churches pray for healing and anoint the sick but do not hold that every sickness will be healed in this life.

uncommon: The Hebrew word for "sickness" in Psalm 103:3 is used in Chronicles of a disease of the bowels.

sections.h: As a father feels for his children (Psalm 103)
sections.b: Psalm 103 is a meditation on God's mercy built on Exodus 34:6, "Compassionate and gracious is the LORD" (Psalm 103:8). It leaves out the creed's warning of punishment, and adds its own pictures: God removes sins as far as sunrise from sunset, and "The way a father feels tenderly for his children / is the way the LORD feels for those who fear him" (Psalm 103:13). The verb racham, "feel tenderly," is related to rechem, "womb." The reason given is human frailty: "he keeps in mind that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14).

Psalms 103 to 106 use chesed again and again: it crowns the forgiven (Psalm 103:4), towers like the heavens (103:11) and lasts from age to age (103:17). Psalm 106 opens with the refrain "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; / his loyal love is forever" (Psalm 106:1) and turns on it: Israel forgot "your many acts of loyal love" (106:7), but God changed his mind, "so many were his acts of loyal love" (106:45). The plural, "acts of loyal love," counts the many times God's faithfulness took concrete form.
sections.refs: Psalm 103:4; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 103:11; Psalm 103:17; Psalm 106:1; Psalm 106:7; Psalm 106:45; 1 Chronicles 16:34

sections.b: The song David's singers sing in 1 Chronicles 16:8–36 is built from Psalm 105:1–15, Psalm 96, and Psalm 106:1 with 106:47–48. Where the Hebrew differs, Chronicles speaks to the people directly ("Keep his covenant in mind," 1 Chronicles 16:15, for the psalm's "He keeps his covenant in mind," Psalm 105:8), names Israel instead of Abraham (1 Chronicles 16:13; Psalm 105:6), expands the prayer to be gathered (1 Chronicles 16:35; Psalm 106:47), and turns the doxology's command into a report that the people said "Amen" (1 Chronicles 16:36; Psalm 106:48). Most scholars think Chronicles borrowed from the Psalter.

Psalm 105:16–22 retells Joseph's story as part of God's plan: God called the famine, but "He had sent someone on before them" (Psalm 105:17), echoing Joseph's words in Genesis 45:5–8. It adds details not in Genesis: fetters on his foot and his neck in iron (105:18), a time of testing by "the LORD's saying" (105:19), and the power to bind Pharaoh's officials and teach his elders (105:22). The Prayer Book line "the iron entered into his soul" comes from the Greek and Latin of 105:18.
sections.refs: Psalm 105:16–22; Genesis 37:28; Genesis 39:20; Genesis 41:40–44; Genesis 45:5–8; Acts 7:9–10

sections.b: Psalm 105:28–36 names eight plagues in its own order: darkness, blood, frogs, the swarm, gnats, hail, locusts and the firstborn. It leaves out the livestock disease and the boils of Exodus 9 and puts darkness, the ninth plague in Exodus, first. Psalm 78:44–51 gives a different selection. Both psalms call the plagues God's "signs" and "wonders" (Psalm 105:27; Psalm 78:43), and Psalm 105 tells them as God's word in action: "He spoke, and the swarm came on" (Psalm 105:31).

Psalm 105 is built on the promise "I will give you the land of Canaan, / the share of your inheritance" (Psalm 105:11), made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob when they were few and foreign, and it ends with the gift: "He handed them the nations' lands" (105:44), so that Israel would keep his laws (105:45). Psalm 106 tells the other side: Israel "rejected the land worth wanting" (106:24), defiled it with blood (106:38), and was scattered from it (106:27, 41), and it ends with a prayer to be gathered (106:47).

sections.b: Psalm 105:40 calls the manna "bread from heaven," as Exodus 16:4 does, and tells the quail and manna as gifts given when the people "asked." Psalm 106:14–15 tells the quail story as a craving punished. In John 6:31 the crowd quotes "He gave them bread from heaven to eat," probably from Psalm 78:24 and Exodus 16, and Jesus answers that he is the true bread from heaven.

In Psalm 105:15 (1 Chronicles 16:22) God's "anointed ones" are Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who were never anointed with oil. The word is used in a wide sense of those God has set apart, and the parallel "my prophets" fits Genesis 20:7, where God calls Abraham a prophet. The verse is often quoted to forbid criticism of church leaders; in context it is God's protection of a vulnerable family against powerful kings.

Psalm 106:19–23 retells the calf at Horeb as an exchange: "They traded their glory / for the shape of an ox that feeds on grass" (Psalm 106:20). Paul echoes the line in Romans 1:23, and Jewish scribal tradition lists the verse among places where an original "my glory" was softened. The psalm credits Moses alone with saving the people: he "stood in the broken wall" before God (106:23).

Psalm 106:23 pictures Moses as a soldier standing in a breach in a city wall, but facing God: he "stood in the broken wall facing him / to turn back his rage from destroying them." Ezekiel 22:30 uses the same image when God finds no one to stand in the gap. Psalm 106:30 adds Phinehas, whose action stopped the plague at Peor.

Psalm 106:28–31 retells the sin at the Baal of Peor and the zeal of Phinehas (Numbers 25:1–13) without describing his spear. It says that Phinehas "rose and gave judgment, / and the plague was held back" (Psalm 106:30), using a verb that may mean judge, intervene or pray. It then says his deed "was reckoned to him as righteousness" (106:31), the words used of Abraham's faith in Genesis 15:6, the only other place with this phrase. 1 Maccabees 2:52–54 joins Abraham and Phinehas in the same way.

Genesis 15:6 says of Abraham's trust, "he reckoned it to him as righteousness," and Paul builds his teaching on justification by faith on that verse (Romans 4:3). Psalm 106:31 uses the same phrase of a deed, Phinehas's zeal at Peor. Catholic readers have pointed to the verse to show that Scripture can call works righteousness; Lutheran and Reformed readers answer that the deed was approved because the person was already accepted by faith. James 2:21–23 and 1 Maccabees 2:52 also join Abraham's faith with his deeds.

Psalm 106:16–18 tells of the revolt against Moses and Aaron in Numbers 16, but names only Dathan and Abiram, as Deuteronomy 11:6 does. Many readers think the silence spares the sons of Korah, the temple singers named in the titles of Psalms 42–49 and 84–88, whose ancestors "did not die" (Numbers 26:11).

Psalm 106:32–33 says the people provoked God "at the waters of Meribah," and "Moses came to harm on their account," because they "defied his spirit" and he spoke rashly. Numbers 20:12 blames Moses' and Aaron's unbelief; the psalm, like Deuteronomy 1:37, stresses the people's part. "His spirit" may be God's Spirit (Isaiah 63:10) or Moses' own.

sections.h: Sons and daughters offered to demons (Psalm 106:37–38)
sections.b: Psalm 106:37–38 says that in the land the Israelites sacrificed their sons and daughters "to demons" and "for Canaan's idols," defiling the land with innocent blood. The word for demons, shedim, appears elsewhere only in Deuteronomy 32:17. The psalm does not name Molech, but it describes the practice that Kings and Jeremiah associate with the Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom.

Psalm 102 hopes for the rebuilding of Zion, whose stones and dust lie in ruins (Psalm 102:13–16), and for the release of prisoners (102:20). Psalm 106 confesses the sins that led to exile, using the words of Solomon's prayer for the exiles ("We have sinned ... We have gone wrong. We have done evil," Psalm 106:6; 1 Kings 8:47), thanks God for making the captors pity them (106:46; 1 Kings 8:50), and prays, "gather us from the nations" (106:47). It also reads the exile back into the wilderness: God swore to scatter the children of the rebels (106:27; Ezekiel 20:23).
sections.refs: Psalm 102:13–22; Psalm 106:6; Psalm 106:27; Psalm 106:46–47; 1 Kings 8:46–50; Ezekiel 20:23

sections.b: Psalm 106 is one of the Bible's great communal confessions, with Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9. It joins the present generation to the sins of its ancestors ("We have sinned along with our ancestors," Psalm 106:6) and tells history honestly as a record of failure, but frames it with thanks for God's loyal love (106:1) and a plea to be saved (106:47).
sections.refs: Psalm 106:6; Psalm 106:47; Ezra 9:6–15; Nehemiah 9:16–37; Daniel 9:4–19; Leviticus 26:40–42

sections.b: "Praise the LORD!" (Hallelu-yah) appears for the first time in the Psalter at the end of Psalm 104 (Psalm 104:35); the Talmud notices this and links it to the downfall of the wicked in the same verse (Bavli Berakhot 9b–10a). Psalm 105 ends with it, and Psalm 106 begins and ends with it. The Greek Psalter moves each Hallelujah to the head of the following psalm as a title, so that Greek Psalms 104, 105 and 106 (Hebrew 105, 106 and 107) are headed "Alleluia."

sections.h: Rebellion at the Sea of Reeds (Psalm 106)
sections.b: Psalm 106:7–12 tells the crossing of the sea as a story of rebellion as well as rescue: Israel "were defiant at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds," yet God "scolded the Sea of Reeds, and it went dry" for the sake of his name (Psalm 106:7–9). The Greek translates Yam Suf as "the Red Sea" here, as everywhere.

The two psalms tell the wilderness years in opposite ways. Psalm 105:39–41 remembers only gifts: the cloud as a shelter, fire for light, quail, bread from heaven and water from the rock. Psalm 106:13–33 remembers only sins: craving, envy of Moses and Aaron, the calf, the rejection of the land, Peor and Meribah. Paul draws on the same episodes as warnings in 1 Corinthians 10:1–11.
